title: "Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts"
subtitle: "Why the graphic says 3-4 and you count four men on the line, why the best run defenses of the light-box era wall off the middle with three big bodies, and how to read a front whose name keeps changing"
description: "The odd fronts from the ground up: what makes a front odd; the 3-4 Okie played two ways (two-gap and one-gap); where the 3-4 came from, presented as the disputed story it is; the stand-up edge; the tite (mint) front and why it walls off inside runs against spread offenses; the nickel fronts (4-2-5, 3-3-5, 2-4-5) and why a roster label and the picture on the field so often disagree; how a front chooses between defending inside and outside zone; multiple defenses, reduced fronts, and the Eagle and G fronts as dialect."
glossary:
  "Odd front": "A defensive front with a lineman head-up on the center (a 0-technique nose), so the line is balanced around the ball; the classic odd fronts have three down linemen (the 3-4, which puts five on the line once its two standing outside linebackers are counted) or five (the old 5-2). In an even front, nobody is head-up on the center."
  "3-4 Okie": "The classic 3-4 alignment, named for Bud Wilkinson's Oklahoma 5-2: a nose head-up on the center, a defensive end on each offensive tackle (head-up in a 4 or outside in a 5), a stand-up outside linebacker at each end of the line and two inside linebackers behind the guards."
  "Tite front": {def: "An odd front with five men on the line: a nose on the center and two defensive linemen in 4i-techniques on the tackles' inside shoulders, with an edge player outside each tackle. The three interior linemen cover the center and both B gaps, walling off inside runs so the linebackers stay unblocked and the defense can keep two safeties deep.", aliases: ["Mint front"]}
  "4-2-5": "A nickel front with four down linemen, two linebackers and five defensive backs; the modern NFL's most common way to line up against three receivers."
  "3-3-5": "A nickel defense with three down linemen, three linebackers and five defensive backs. As an NFL front call it means a five-man line in nickel (three interior linemen, two stand-up edges, one linebacker), the tite of a 3-4 team's nickel; as a roster count it usually just means a four-man line with one edge listed as an end and the other as a linebacker; the college 3-3-5 stack is a different defense again."
  "2-4-5": "A nickel front with two down linemen, four linebackers and five defensive backs: usually a 3-4 team's nickel, with the nose off the field and the two outside linebackers on the edges, so it looks like a four-man line."
  "Stand-up edge": {def: "An edge player who lines up at the end of the line of scrimmage standing in a two-point stance instead of with a hand on the ground, so he can rush the passer, set the edge against the run or drop into coverage; in 3-4 defenses he is called an outside linebacker.", aliases: ["Outside linebacker (3-4)"]}
  "Multiple defense": {def: "A defense that lines up in more than one front family (odd and even, three, four and five men on the line), often from the same personnel and sometimes shifting between them before the snap, so its base label says little about what you will see.", aliases: ["Hybrid defense"]}
  "Reduced front": "A front in which the defensive linemen on one side (or both) slide a gap inward from their usual spots, for example an end moving from a 5-technique to a 3 or a 4i, with an edge player on the line outside them to take the outside gap; the 4-3 Under is the classic one-side reduction and the tite front reduces both sides."
  "Eagle front": "A front name that means different things in different eras and staffs: Greasy Neale's 1940s Philadelphia Eagles five-man line, Fritz Shurmur's linebacker-heavy package with the 1980s Rams, and, in modern 3-4 playbooks, either an Okie whose ends pinch inside to 4i-techniques (what other staffs call a tite or mint front) or a one-side change-up in which an outside linebacker walks up onto the tackle and the end beside him reduces inside."
  "G front": "A front tag that moves the nose off the center onto a guard's inside shoulder (a 2i-technique, 'G' for guard), changing the blocking angles for the center and the guard on inside runs."

`````` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"}
import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import os
import re
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style
from gridiron.play import draw_marker

GREEN = "#0f7a55"         # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
OL_KEYS = ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line(labels="full"):
    """The five offensive linemen, labelled LT..RT ("full") or with one letter, T G C G T ("short")."""
    short = {"LT": "T", "LG": "G", "C": "C", "RG": "G", "RT": "T"}
    return [p.moved(label=(p.key if labels == "full" else short[p.key])) for p in offense("singleback")
            if p.key in OL_KEYS]


def te(side=1, key=None, label=None):
    """An in-line tight end: Y on the right, U on the left."""
    key = key or ("Y" if side > 0 else "U")
    return O(key, "TE", -0.7, side * 4.8, label or key)


def T(t, side=1):
    """Width of technique t on the offense's right (side=+1) or left (side=-1)."""
    return technique(t, side)


def gun11(y_attached=True):
    """Shotgun, 11 personnel: Y attached on the right (or flexed to a slot), H in the left slot, X and Z wide."""
    sk = [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
          O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
    sk.append(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y") if y_attached else O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0, "Y"))
    return line("full") + sk


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, path, run or motion."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "motion":
        return p.motion(key, pts=pts, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def gap_tag(fld, p, d, w, text, color=GREEN, fontsize=8.5):
    """A gap letter in a small rounded box."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                fontweight="bold", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=1.0))


def spot(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ms=10):
    """Mark a point (a tackle, a meeting point) with an X."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=ms, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)


def lane(fld, p, w0, w1, d0, d1, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10, ls=(0, (3, 2))):
    """Shade a rectangular lane (a run lane, a gap) from width w0 to w1 and depth d0 to d1."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=color, alpha=alpha,
                               ec=color, lw=0.9, ls=ls, zorder=0.8))


def dashed(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, lw=1.5, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed 'what if' or 'intent' path through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    xs, ys = np.asarray(xs, float), np.asarray(ys, float)
    if end == "arrow":
        hx, hy = xs[-2] + 0.75 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.75 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])
        xs = np.concatenate([xs[:-1], [hx, xs[-1]]]); ys = np.concatenate([ys[:-1], [hy, ys[-1]]])
        fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))
    else:
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)


def bracket(fld, p, d, w0, w1, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=2.0):
    """A bar spanning the gaps a defender owns, with end ticks."""
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = _P(fld, p, d, w0), _P(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb], color=color, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=5)
    for w in (w0, w1):
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d - 0.32, w), _P(fld, p, d + 0.32, w)
        fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=lw, zorder=5)


def hand(fld, p, d, w, half=0.66):
    """A hand on the ground: a dark knob on the front edge of a defender's square marker."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d - half, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.26, fc=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))


def hands(fld, p, keys, t=None, half=0.66):
    for k in keys:
        d, w = (p.players[k].d, p.players[k].w) if t is None else p.position(k, t)
        hand(fld, p, d, w, half)


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip anything outside the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:   # yard numbers, not technique labels
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, keep_numbers=False, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    if not keep_numbers:
        clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def front(spec, lbs=(), others=()):
    """Defensive linemen from (key, technique, side) triples, labelled with their technique number,
    plus (key, d, w, label) linebackers / edges and any other defenders."""
    out = [D(k, "DL", 1.0, T(t, s), t) for k, t, s in spec]
    out += [D(k, "LB", d, w, lab) for k, d, w, lab in lbs]
    out += [D(k, "S", d, w, lab) for k, d, w, lab in others]
    return out


def secondary(nickel_w=None, high=11.5, safety_w=7.5):
    """Two corners on X and Z, two deep safeties and (optionally) a nickel back at apex width."""
    out = [D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "C"),
           D("FS", "FS", high, -safety_w, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", high, safety_w, "SS")]
    if nickel_w is not None:
        out.append(D("NB", "NB", 4.6, nickel_w, "$"))
    return out


def box_outline(fld, p, w0, w1, d0=-0.2, d1=6.6, text=None, text_at=None):
    """The box, as a faint dashed outline, with an optional count label."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc="none",
                               ec=style.MUTED, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 2.5)), zorder=1.5))
    if text:
        say(fld, p, *(text_at or (d1 + 0.9, (w0 + w1) / 2)), text, color=style.INK, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web) for the simulated plays --------------------------------------
MARK_R = 0.62


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), enter=(), ring_r=0.85, relabel=None):
    """One moment of a simulated play on `ax`: markers, trails of on-screen players, rings.
    `relabel(key, t)` may return a new label for a player at time t (a lineman who changes technique)."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    snap = df[df["frameId"] == int((tmap - 0.0).abs().idxmin())]
    first = snap[snap["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.8, play.los + window[1] - 0.8)
                 & snap["y"].between(ylo + 0.8, yhi - 0.8)]
    ids = set(first["_id"]) | {"football"}
    inside = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0], play.los + window[1]) & cur["y"].between(ylo, yhi)]
    ids |= set(inside["_id"]) & set(enter)
    shown = cur[cur["_id"].isin(ids) | (cur["side"] == "ball")]
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=9))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if relabel is not None and r["side"] == "def":
            lab = relabel(str(r["displayName"]), t) or lab
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), ring_r, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.6, zorder=7))
    for patch in ax.patches:
        patch.set_clip_on(True)
    return fld


def strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=5.2, after=None, enter=(),
          relabel=None):
    """Numbered frame strip. `moments` is a list of (play, t, tag)."""
    cache = {}
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(moments) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.62 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(moments):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, (play, t, tag)) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, moments)):
        if id(play) not in cache:
            cache[id(play)] = tracking(play)
        fld = panel(ax, play, cache[id(play)], t, lateral, window, rings, enter, relabel=relabel)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, i)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}" + (f"   {tag}" if tag else ""), fontsize=8.3, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.1, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.3 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(segments, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=4.6, after=None, enter=(), relabel=None):
    """Web version: each (play, tag, [(t, note), ...]) segment played in turn, notes as captions."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.45))
    frames = []
    for play, tag, notes in segments:
        df = tracking(play)
        tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
        frames += [(play, df, float(tmap[f]), tag, notes) for f in sorted(df["frameId"].unique())]

    def update(k):
        play, df, t, tag, notes = frames[k]
        ax.clear()
        fld = panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, enter, relabel=relabel)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, -1)
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (f"  {tag}" if tag else "")
        cur = [n for tt, n in notes if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        ax.set_title(txt + (("\n" + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""), fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK,
                     loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=range(len(frames)), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(moments, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), after=None, enter=(), ncols=2, width_in=5.2,
                       relabel=None):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=notes, rings=rings, ncols=ncols, width_in=width_in,
              after=after, enter=enter, relabel=relabel)
        plt.show()
        return
    segs = []
    for play, t, tag in moments:
        if not segs or segs[-1][0] is not play:
            segs.append((play, tag, []))
    for (play, t, tag), n in zip(moments, notes):
        for s in segs:
            if s[0] is play:
                s[2].append((t, n))
    video(segs, lateral, window, rings=rings, after=after, enter=enter, relabel=relabel)
``````

The graphic in the corner of the screen says the defense is in a **3-4**. You count. Four players at
the line of scrimmage, two of them standing up, two with a hand on the ground. Next snap, after a
substitution you barely notice (a huge man jogging on, a linebacker jogging off), there are *five*
across the line, three of them enormous and wedged inside the offensive tackles, with a single
linebacker behind them. The offense hands the ball to its
running back on an inside run, the kind that worked all afternoon last week, and he runs into a wall
two yards deep. No blocker ever touched the linebacker. "That's their tite front," says the analyst.
"Three big bodies inside, and nobody can get to the second level." So which is it: a 3-4, a four-man
line, a five-man line? And how did a defense with only six men near the ball stop a run aimed at six
blockers? This chapter is about the other family of fronts, the *odd* ones, and about why, in the
modern game, the names on the graphic tell you less than the picture on the field.

**You'll be able to:**

- Look at a front before the snap, find whether anyone is head-up on the center, and say whether it is
  odd or even.
- Diagram the 3-4 Okie, and tell from the linemen's alignment and first step whether it is being played
  two-gap (control and read) or one-gap (attack).
- Recognize a tite (or mint) front, explain why it walls off inside runs against spread offenses, and
  name what it gives up.
- Identify the nickel fronts (4-2-5, 3-3-5, 2-4-5) by counting hands on the ground and players
  standing on the edges, and explain why a roster label and the picture so often disagree.
- Explain how a defense picks a front to stop inside zone and a different one to stop outside zone.
- Decode front dialect (Okie, Eagle, G, reduced) and know when one word means different things in
  different buildings.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd)**: an **even front** has nobody head-up on the center (the
  4-3 *Over* puts its 3-technique toward the tight end, the *Under* away from him), and every even front
  has a rule, usually tied to the tight end, that tells you where the linemen will line up.
- **[Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)**: technique numbers from the
  defense's side (the 0 nose, the 3, the 4i, 4 and 5 on the tackle, the 9 and the wide-9), one-gap
  versus two-gap, setting the edge and contain.
- **[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)**: base
  defenses (the [4-3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4-3) and the [3-4](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-4)),
  [nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel), the [box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box) and
  the [light box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box), and [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high)
  safety shells.
- **[Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)**: inside and outside zone, double teams
  that climb to linebackers, and the cutback.
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** As in the rest of Part 5: offense is blue circles, defense orange squares,
plays go up the page, and *left* and *right* are always the offense's left and right. Defensive linemen
are labelled with their **technique number** (a 0 is a nose head-up on the center, a 4i is on a
tackle's inside shoulder). **E** is an *edge* player standing up at the end of the line; **M** and **W**
are inside linebackers; **$** is the nickel back; **C** a cornerback; **FS** and **SS** the safeties.
Offensive linemen are **LT, LG, C, RG, RT**, shortened to **T G C G T** in the smaller panels; **R** is
the running back and **F** a fullback. New in this chapter: **a dark dot on the front edge of a defender's square is a hand on the ground.**
A square with no dot is a player standing up. Counting dots is how you will tell fronts apart, because
counting players stopped working a long time ago.

## Odd and even: who is on the center?

Every front in football starts with one question, and you can answer it from the couch: **is anybody
lined up head-up on the center?**

If nobody is head-up on the center, the front is **even**: the defensive tackles line up on or around
the guards, the center is *uncovered* or only shaded, and you are looking at one of the four-man fronts
of [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd). If a big man stands right over the ball, nose to nose with the
center, the front is [**odd**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-odd-front): it is balanced around a
**0-technique** nose tackle. The classic odd fronts have three down linemen (the 3-4, which puts five on
the line once you count its two standing outside linebackers) or five (the old 5-2), rather than four.

Why does one alignment decide the family? Because of what it does to the offensive line's
arithmetic. In an even front, nobody is square in front of the center: at most a tackle shaded on one of
his shoulders, a man he can work on together with a guard, and often nobody at all, in which case he is free
to help or to climb to a linebacker. The defense has eased the center's job in exchange for putting its
tackles where they can attack the guards. In an odd front, the center has a man in his face on every
snap, and a nose head-up on him is responsible for *both* A gaps, one on each side of the center. The
center can't block him alone at a good angle in either direction, so one of the two guards usually has
to help. That is the founding idea of every odd front: **put a heavy man on
the center, make the offense spend two blockers on him, and let somebody else run free.** You met that
nose in [Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd). This chapter is about the fronts
built around him.

A warning before we start, which the rest of the chapter will keep proving: "odd" and "even" describe
*where linemen stand*, not *who is on the roster*. A team that calls itself a 3-4 team plays an even
front on plenty of snaps, and a 4-3 team can put a nose on the center. Keep your eyes on the center.

## The 3-4 Okie

The [**3-4 Okie**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-4-okie) is the classic 3-4, the one drawn in
every coaching book: a nose head-up on the center, a defensive end on each offensive tackle, a
[stand-up edge](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stand-up-edge) at each end of the line, and two inside
linebackers behind the guards. The name is short for *Oklahoma*, because the alignment is Bud
Wilkinson's Oklahoma 5-2 of the late 1940s and 1950s with its two outside men standing up (more on that
history below).

Read @fig-okie-plate as a list of jobs, the way you learned to in
[Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd).

- **The nose** takes on the center, and very often a guard as well. He is usually the heaviest man on
  the defense, because his whole value is in not moving.
- **The ends** sit on the offensive tackles. In the classic version they are head-up there, in a
  4-technique, and they control the tackle and play the gap on either side of him. Others line up on
  the tackle's outside shoulder, a 5. They are long and strong, the 290-to-320-pound bodies built to
  lock out a tackle at arm's length.
- **The outside linebackers** are standing up at each end of the line. Against the run they set the
  edge; against the pass, one or both rush; and on some snaps one drops into coverage. They are the
  lightest players in the front, edge rushers in all but stance.
- **The inside linebackers** stand behind the guards, and here is the design's point. Count the
  offensive linemen who don't have a defender on or near them before the snap: the two guards. In
  zone-blocking terms they are *uncovered* ([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)),
  and an uncovered guard wants to climb straight to a linebacker. The Okie's whole design is to make
  that impossible: the nose is too much for the center alone, so one guard has to stay and help; the
  ends hold the tackles so they can't climb either. If the front does its job, at most one blocker
  reaches the second level, and two linebackers are left to make tackles.

### One alignment, two ways to play it

What the front does after the snap is a separate choice from where it lines up. A 3-4 can be a
*two-gap* front, in which the three linemen control blockers and read, or a *one-gap* front, in which
every defender attacks a gap at the snap. You learned the difference player by player in
[Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd). Here is what each looks like across the
whole front.

**The two-gap 3-4** is the old-school version, and its appeal is the math in the left half of
@fig-okie-two-ways. Three linemen can hold six gaps if each of them can stand up a blocker and play
either side of him. That leaves the two inside linebackers *gap-free*: they don't have to guess at the
snap; they watch the play develop and run to the ball, and the linemen in front of them keep the
blockers off them. (Against one back, that is. Against a fullback, like the one in @fig-okie-plate, the
offense has an extra blocker who can lead through a hole, and one inside linebacker has to meet him
there while the other fills off the nose; [Linebackers](05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd) has
that fight.) Bill Parcells's New York Giants of the 1980s played it, with Bill Belichick as his
defensive coordinator, and Belichick's New England Patriots of the 2000s played it with linemen like
Vince Wilfork, Richard Seymour and Ty Warren, all built like the job: big, long and patient.[^bigthree]

The cost, as [Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd) explained, is that
two-gappers are always reacting. They rarely make plays behind the line or sack the quarterback, they
need bodies the draft produces only a few of each year, and on passing downs the defense usually has to
take the nose off for someone quicker.

**The one-gap 3-4** keeps the personnel and changes the job. Line the ends up shaded into gaps, shade
the nose, and tell every defender to attack his gap at the snap, and the 3-4 becomes an attacking
front. The right half of @fig-okie-two-ways shows the most common way to do it, and it holds a secret:
lined up this way, a "3-4" is almost exactly the 4-3 Under of [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd), a
nose shaded to the tight end, a 3-technique away from him, a 5 and a 9 to the tight end's side, with the
Sam linebacker called an outside linebacker and standing up. Run this chapter's one-glance test on it:
nobody is head-up on the center any more, so by alignment this "3-4" is an *even* front.

That is why "3-4" by itself is a weak clue. The number of linemen tells you how many there are; their
alignment and **first step** tell you how they play. A two-gapper's first step goes *into the blocker*,
hands first, and he stays at the line. A one-gapper's goes *into a gap*, and he is across the line
before the blocker has finished his first step. Watch the ends for two snaps and you will know which 3-4
you are watching.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**The 3-4 trades linemen for linebackers, and two-gap play is what makes that trade affordable.** Take a
defensive lineman off the field and put a linebacker on, and you gain a player who can rush, drop into
coverage or fill a run lane, and who keeps the offense guessing which of those he'll do. You lose one big
body at the line. The two-gap 3-4 covers the loss with technique: three linemen hold six gaps, and the
linebackers run free. The one-gap 3-4 covers it with movement and speed: every man attacks, and the
extra linebacker is just one more fast player who can come from anywhere. Either way, the defense is
betting that a fourth linebacker is worth more than a fourth lineman. In an era of spread offenses,
three-receiver sets and quarterbacks who throw on first down, that bet has mostly paid.
:::

## Where the 3-4 came from (and why nobody agrees)

Ask who invented the 3-4 and you will get at least four answers, each true about something. The honest
version is a family tree, not a birth certificate.

**The ancestors: five men on the line.** In 1947 Earle "Greasy" Neale, the Philadelphia Eagles' head
coach, built his defense around a five-man line with two linebackers behind it. It was called the
[Eagle defense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-eagle-front), and the Eagles won NFL championships
with it in 1948 and 1949.[^neale] Bud Wilkinson took the five-man line to the University of Oklahoma,
where it became the *Oklahoma 5-2*, the defense behind his Sooners'
47-game winning streak in the 1950s. (That is where *Okie* comes from.) Now look at a 5-2 the way a
coach of the 1970s did. The two men at the ends of the line were defensive ends, but they were usually
smaller and quicker than the three linemen inside them, and their jobs were to set the edge and, on some
plays, to drop. Stand them up, call them linebackers, and the same seven players become three linemen
and four linebackers. Nobody had to invent the 3-4; it was hiding inside the 5-2.[^okla]

**The NFL arrivals, early 1970s: several claimants.**

- **Bill Arnsparger, Miami, 1972.** The Dolphins' defensive coordinator under Don Shula had a
  linebacker, Bob Matheson, who could play with his hand on the ground or standing up. Arnsparger moved
  him around the front, sometimes as a fourth linebacker, sometimes as a rushing end, and the package
  was named for his jersey: the **[53 defense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-53-defense)**. The
  Dolphins went 17–0. Was it a 3-4? On some snaps, yes, and it is often named as the 3-4's NFL
  ancestor; the story belongs to [The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd).[^matheson]
- **Chuck Fairbanks, New England, 1974.** Fairbanks had coached the Oklahoma 5-2 as the Sooners' head
  coach, and when he took over the Patriots he brought it with him, standing up its ends. His 1974
  Patriots are usually named as the first NFL team to use the 3-4 as their regular base defense.[^fairbanks]
- **Bum Phillips, Houston, 1974–75.** Phillips, the cowboy-hatted Texan who had devised the technique
  numbers you have been using since [The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd),
  was the Oilers' defensive coordinator under Sid Gillman, and had talked Gillman into a 3-4, when they
  traded for nose tackle Curley Culp in October 1974; he kept the 3-4 when he became head coach in
  January 1975. Culp, a former NCAA heavyweight wrestling champion at Arizona State, was strong enough
  to need two blockers, and Phillips gave him the credit: "Curley made [the 3-4 defense] work. He made
  me look smart."[^culp]

**The boom and the bust.** Within a few years the 3-4 was everywhere. John Madden's Raiders switched to
it in 1976, after injuries thinned their defensive line, and won the Super Bowl; Arnsparger's Dolphins
went to it full time in 1977; and by the late 1970s and early 1980s it was the league's most common base
defense.[^boom] Then offenses changed again, the one-back passing games of the 1980s and 1990s made
four-man fronts with fast defensive ends fashionable, and by the mid-1990s only a handful of teams,
most notably Buffalo and Pittsburgh, still lined up in a 3-4. The revival came in the 2000s, led by the Steelers and
Belichick's Patriots, and took a new shape that the rest of this chapter is about: the stand-up edge
rusher, the one-gap 3-4, and in the 2020s the five-man tite front. The longer arc, including the 3-4's
role in the rise of the [hybrid edge](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hybrid-edge) (the stand-up
edge below, treated as a position of its own: part end, part linebacker), is in
[Dynasties and Counterpunches](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd) and
[The Single Wing to the Scoring Drought](../11-history/11-01-single-wing-to-scoring-drought.qmd).

So who invented it? Wilkinson's 5-2 supplied the alignment, Arnsparger the idea of a hybrid
end-linebacker, Fairbanks and Phillips the commitment to it as a base defense, and Madden the Super Bowl
that sold it. That is the usual shape of football history: a problem (offenses running more and
throwing more on early downs), several smart people solving it in the same few years, and credit that
depends on whom you ask.

## The stand-up edge

The 3-4's most important legacy isn't the nose. It is the player at the end of the line who isn't
sure whether he is a lineman or a linebacker, and doesn't need to be.

A [**stand-up edge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stand-up-edge) lines up at the end of the line of
scrimmage in a two-point stance, standing, instead of with a hand in the dirt. In a 3-4 he is called an
[**outside linebacker**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-outside-linebacker-3-4), and the roster lists him
that way; on the field, most snaps, he is an [edge rusher](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-edge-rusher)
doing a defensive end's job. Lawrence Taylor in the 1980s, Kevin Greene and Greg Lloyd in the 1990s,
DeMarcus Ware and Von Miller in the 2000s and 2010s, T.J. Watt today: the most feared pass rushers of
the 3-4 era stood up.

**Why stand?** Three reasons, each a trade.

1. **Vision and options.** Standing, he sees the whole backfield, and he can move in any direction at
   the snap: rush, take on a blocker, or turn and drop into coverage. A lineman in a three-point stance,
   weight forward on his hand, is committed to going forward. The offense can't rule out a drop from a
   standing edge, so it can't be sure who is rushing. That uncertainty is the seed of the
   [simulated pressures](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd) of Part 7: four-man
   rushes in which a lineman drops into coverage and a player the offense didn't count rushes instead.
2. **Width and a view of the tackle.** Standing, he can align wider and watch how the tackle sets before
   he commits to an inside or outside move. It isn't a free win: plenty of rushers still prefer a hand
   down for a faster get-off on obvious passing downs.
3. **Disguise.** A front with two standing edges can become a four-man line, a five-man line or a
   three-man rush without anyone substituting. That is the trick behind the opening of this chapter,
   and it gets its own animation below.

**What it costs.** Mostly leverage against the run. A defender in a three-point stance comes out low,
and the low man wins at the line; a standing edge has to sink as he takes on a tackle or a tight end, or
he gets pushed upfield and the edge goes soft. That is why the stand-up edges who last are the ones who
can set the edge as well as rush (in [Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)'s
terms, who keep their outside arm free against a 300-pound tackle), and why many of them put a hand down
in short yardage and at the goal line, where leverage is everything. The most common hand-down moment of
all is on passing downs in nickel, when the 3-4 outside linebacker becomes, in everything but the roster,
a 4-2-5's defensive end (more on that below). The body type is in between, too: usually 245 to 265 pounds, lighter than a
defensive end, heavier than an inside linebacker. Teams that play four-man fronts draft the same
players and call them defensive ends. The player is the same; the label follows the scheme.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A 3-4 outside linebacker is a linebacker, so he covers people." Some do, some of the time. Most of
the great ones spend the large majority of their passing-down snaps rushing the quarterback. When you
see a 3-4 outside linebacker drop into coverage, it is usually a deliberate surprise, designed to put
a defender where the quarterback expected an empty space, not his everyday job.
:::

## The Phillips branch: the attacking 3-4

The 3-4's revival in the 2000s split along the line from @fig-okie-two-ways. Belichick's Patriots and the
Steelers kept versions that leaned on two-gap play up front. The other branch came from one family,
the Phillipses.

Wade Phillips, Bum's son and his linebackers coach in Houston from 1976 to 1980, spent four decades as a
coordinator and head coach running his father's 3-4, and running it the attacking way, not the
two-gap way the Parcells and Belichick branch made famous.[^wade] Phillips's linemen were shaded into
gaps and attacked them; his outside linebackers rushed; the ends were penetrators, not anchors. When he took over the
Houston Texans' defense in 2011, the team's own preview called it "his one-gap scheme," and the line
coach said it was "not like a two-gap type defense where you need that 350-pound nose man."[^phillips34]
The proof arrived the following year, when the Texans' 5-technique end, J.J. Watt, led the league with
20.5 sacks and was Defensive Player of the Year: the end of a 3-4, the position that used to exist to
let linebackers make tackles, had become the defense's best pass rusher.[^watt]

Four years later Phillips took the same ideas to Denver, where the 2015 Broncos allowed the fewest yards
in the league and won Super Bowl 50 with two stand-up edges, Von Miller and DeMarcus Ware, chasing the
quarterback.[^sb50] Their film room is below.

A two-gap 3-4 and a one-gap 3-4 use the same eleven bodies and ask opposite things of them. The modern
descendants of both branches meet in one front, which is next: it has a two-gap nose like Belichick's and
one-gap linemen beside him like Phillips's.

## The tite front: walling off the middle

The [**tite front**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tite-front) is an odd front with five men on
the line: a nose on the center, two defensive linemen in **4i-techniques** on the inside shoulders of
the offensive tackles, and an edge player outside each tackle. Fangio and his coaching tree call it
*tite*; Kirby Smart's Georgia calls the same picture the
[**mint front**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mint-front); and, as the dialect section below shows,
some playbooks call it *Eagle*.

It is a [**reduced front**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reduced-front) on both sides. In a
reduced front, the defensive linemen slide a gap inward from their usual spots and an edge player takes
the outside gap they left. The 4-3 Under of [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd) reduces one side (its
backside end moves down toward the guard); the tite takes the Okie and reduces *both* ends, from the
tackles' outside shoulders (5s) to their inside shoulders (4is). That one move inside is the whole
front.

Why move the ends *inside*? Put a nose on the center and a 4i in each B gap, and the whole interior of
the line, from one tackle's inside shoulder to the other's, has a big body in it. Now run the
covered-or-uncovered test from [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) for inside zone
to the offense's right. The center is covered (the nose is on him), the right guard is covered (the 4i is
on his play side) and so is the left tackle. The left guard and the right tackle are *uncovered*, and in
an ordinary front those are the two men who would climb to linebackers. Here they can't, because each
stands next to a defender who can't be blocked one-on-one: the left guard has to help the center with the
nose, and the right tackle has to help the right guard with the 4i. The offense can still double-team,
but every double team is spent on a lineman, and every blocker who stays on a lineman is a blocker who
isn't on a linebacker.

If that sounds like the bear front of [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd), it should: both fronts decide
that no interior blocker will be free. The bear does it by covering the center and both guards (a 0 and
two 3s), and the 46 that made it famous put eight men near the ball to fill everything else. The tite
sits on the center and the tackles' inside shoulders, which does the same job against the inside runs
with five on the line and two safeties still deep. The price of that choice, as we'll see, is the space outside the tackles, where the bear had
bodies and the tite has only its edges.

Here is the tite doing its job against the most common run in football, inside zone.

::: {#cell-fig-tite-inside-zone .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def tite_iz():
    off = gun11(y_attached=True)
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
           D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.1, "E"),
           D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")] + secondary(nickel_w=-6.2, high=11.0, safety_w=7.6)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    # doubles: C + LG on the nose, RG + RT on the play-side 4i; they hold, nobody climbs.
    # (blockers stop about 1.25 yd short of their man, centre to centre: contact, with both labels readable)
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.35, 0.3), speed=1.4); go_to(p, "LG", (-0.35, -1.0), speed=1.6, via=[(-0.6, -1.3)])
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.9, -0.05), "path", speed=0.6)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.3, 1.95), speed=1.6, via=[(-0.55, 1.75)]); go_to(p, "RT", (-0.3, 3.25), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "R4", (0.9, 2.6), "path", speed=0.5)
    # the left tackle cuts off the backside 4i; the backside edge squeezes but stays square (he has the QB)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.3, -2.3), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "L4", (0.9, -2.35), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "LE", (0.7, -4.0), "path", speed=1.2, delay=0.2)
    # the tight end blocks the play-side edge, who holds the edge
    go_to(p, "Y", (-0.3, 5.0), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "RE", (0.9, 6.1), "path", speed=0.4)
    # the Mike reads and fills the C gap; the strong safety comes down; the nickel holds his slot
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.7, 2.3), "path", speed=3.6, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.1, 4.4), "path", speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "SS", (4.0, 5.4), "path", speed=5.6, delay=0.45)
    go_to(p, "FS", (9.6, -5.2), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.5)
    go_to(p, "NB", (4.0, -6.0), "path", speed=0.8, delay=0.3)
    # the QB rides the mesh and carries out a keep fake; the back presses the B gap, bends outside the tackle
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.1, -0.4), "path", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, -3.0), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.15)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.9, 2.15), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-4.7, -0.2), (-3.8, 1.4)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (0.8, 4.35), "run", speed=5.5)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.5)
    return p


def tite_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    hands(fld, play, ("L4", "NT", "R4"), t=t, half=0.57)
    if t >= 1.45:
        spot(fld, play, 1.45, 3.4, ms=8)


P_TITE = tite_iz()
animation_or_strip([(P_TITE, 0.0, ""), (P_TITE, 0.5, ""), (P_TITE, 1.0, ""), (P_TITE, 1.5, "")],
                   notes=["five on the line, one LB:\nsix in the box vs six blockers",
                          "both doubles stuck on a\nlineman: nobody climbs",
                          "the B gap is full;\nthe back bends outside",
                          "the unblocked Mike fills\nthe C gap: about a yard"],
                   rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-7.8, 8.6), window=(-6.6, 7.2),
                   after=tite_marks, width_in=5.4, enter=("SS",))
```

Walk through @fig-tite-inside-zone with the zone rules from
[Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) in mind. Inside zone wins with double teams: two
linemen drive a defensive lineman backward, and when the linebacker behind commits, one of them comes
off and blocks him. That requires two things: a lineman the pair can move, and a linebacker within
reach. The tite takes away both.

- **The doubles can't move their men.** The nose plays the center *and* whichever guard joins the double:
  what analysts of these light-box fronts call "gap-and-a-half" play, in which a big two-gap nose
  controls one A gap and leans into the other.[^tite] The 4i sits in the B gap, exactly where inside
  zone's aiming point is, so the right guard and the right tackle have to block him together. Neither can
  come off to climb: the 4i is already *in* the hole, so the moment one of them leaves, the man who
  stays is blocking him from the wrong side and the hole closes.
- **Nobody climbs.** With every blocker spent on a lineman, the one inside linebacker is never touched.
  That doesn't mean he has no job. He owns a gap like everyone else (the next section counts them), but
  he can fill it without having to beat a block first, and the wall in front of him has already told the
  running back where *not* to go.
- **The cutback is plugged.** Inside zone's best friend is the bend back to the weak side. In the tite,
  the backside A and B gaps have the nose and the backside 4i in them, and the backside edge is
  squeezing down the line behind them. He squeezes *square*, though, not flat down the line: against a
  shotgun team the quarterback can pull the ball and run where the edge just left, so the edge closes
  the gap without giving up the quarterback.

What's left for the runner is outside the tackle, and here it matters *how* he gets there. A **bounced**
inside run is late and alone: the back has pressed the B gap, stopped, and turned, and while he did, the
Mike, the play-side edge and a safety coming down have had a full second to get there. That is the trade
the tite offers on purpose. **It turns the inside runs that win against two-high defenses into bounced
runs that its linebacker and safeties can chase down.** A run *designed* to go outside is a different
matter, because it arrives with its blockers already out there. That is the tite's weak spot, and we'll
come to it.

### Why the tite exists now: six men, seven gaps

The tite has existed in college for a long time, but it took over the NFL conversation in the late 2010s
for a reason you have met before: two deep safeties. Defenses facing modern passing offenses want to
keep both safeties deep, as long as possible
([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) has the
numbers: split-safety looks reached a record 42 percent of dropbacks in 2025).[^twohigh] Two safeties
deep and five defensive backs on the field leaves six men in the box. Against an offense with a tight
end attached, that is six defenders for six blockers and seven gaps. By the one-man-per-gap accounting
of one-gap football, the numbers don't work.

::: {#cell-fig-tite-gaps .cell execution_count=6}

@fig-tite-gaps shows how the tite makes the numbers work. One nose who holds both A gaps is the extra
defender the box doesn't have: five men on the line take six of the seven gaps, the Mike takes the last
one without a blocker in his way, and the safeties can stay home on the pass and fit the run late, from
depth, with the [alley](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-alley-player) outside the edges left to a
safety or the nickel. The 4is are one-gap players (each has his B gap), but they play it from an inside shade, by
locking onto the tackle rather than darting past him, which is why they need the length and strength of
two-gappers.[^bgaps] The assignments vary by staff and by how many linebackers are on the field. A
college tite with two inside linebackers often lets the nose play just one A gap, the one away from the
center's first step, with a linebacker filling the other;[^galina] the NFL's nickel tite, with one
linebacker, leans on the nose to hold both.

The Fangio tree, Vic Fangio himself and the coaches who worked under him, Brandon Staley among them,
built their light-box run defense on exactly that bargain. Fangio's 2018 Chicago Bears, his last season
as a coordinator before he became Denver's head coach, played their 3-4, often in the tite, with big
interior linemen (Akiem Hicks and the nose Eddie Goldman) and two stand-up edges (Leonard Floyd and Khalil
Mack, acquired in a trade the week before the season), and allowed the fewest points in the league (283)
while leading it in takeaways (36).[^bears18] The light-box bargain is clearest in Staley's 2020 Rams,
who by one count played a light box on about 78 percent of snaps, the second-highest rate in the league,
and allowed the fewest points in the NFL (296).[^staley] Fangio himself is still at it: he is the
Eagles' defensive coordinator in 2026, his third season there.[^fangio26]

### What the tite gives up

Every front is a trade. The tite's costs are specific, and offenses know them.

- **The pass rush.** Three of its five linemen are big interior players built to hold blocks, not beat
  them; the 4is especially are aligned to take the run away, not to rush. To get four rushers, the tite
  often has to rush both edges and two interior men, or send an off-ball linebacker. Cody Alexander, one
  of the most widely read writers on defensive structure, names this as the front's main drawback: "its
  inability to get a rush without sending an off-ball defender."[^alexander]
- **The perimeter.** With three big bodies inside the tackles, the defense outside them is thin: one
  edge on each side, a linebacker flowing from the middle, and safeties coming from depth. Runs that are
  *designed* to start outside, outside zone, tosses, the jet sweeps of
  [Perimeter and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd), arrive there
  with blockers in front of them and go straight at that thinness. The next section shows how.
- **Angles for gap runs.** Linemen lined up inside their blockers hand a gap scheme easy *down* blocks:
  on power to the right, the right tackle blocks down on the 4i and the right guard down on the nose, both
  from the side. The tite survives power with technique, not alignment: the 4i squeezes the down block
  and closes the B gap anyway, the edge meets the pulling guard and spills the ball back inside, and the
  lone linebacker fits off the spill. If any of the three loses, there is nobody behind them but
  safeties. ([Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) draws a full fit against power.)
- **The quick game and the RPO.** A light box with a single linebacker leaves big spaces underneath. The
  [RPO](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) was built for exactly this defender: a lone linebacker who
  must fill the run will leave the space behind him open for a throw.
- **Rare players, again.** Like the two-gap 3-4, the tite needs a nose who can hold two blockers and two
  4is with the length to play from an inside shade. The front is only as good as those three men.

Two practical notes before we leave it. First, the tite is balanced, so unlike the Over and Under it has
no strength call for its interior: the 0 and the two 4is stay put wherever the tight end lines up, and
only the edges and the Mike adjust (the edge on the tight end's side widens to his outside shoulder, and
the Mike's gap goes with him). Second, when the offense detaches its tight end and goes 2x2 or empty,
there are only five blockers and six gaps, and the five-man line covers all six by itself, so the Mike
becomes a truly free player. That sounds ideal, but those formations are usually passing formations, and
a five-man line that rushes four is exactly the problem in the first bullet above, which is one reason
defenses so often meet them with a four-man front instead.

## Inside zone or outside zone? How a front chooses

The tite is the clearest example of a principle that runs through all of defensive front design, and
it is the best way to understand why a defense changes fronts from week to week: **every alignment makes
some blocks easier and others harder, and a defense picks the alignment that makes the offense's
favourite blocks hard.**

Recall the two zone plays from [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd):

- **Inside zone** is won by *double teams* that move a defensive lineman back and then *climb* to a
  linebacker. Its aiming point is the play-side B gap.
- **Outside zone** is won by *reach blocks*: each blocker steps sideways and tries to get his head
  outside the defender in front of him. Its aiming point is the tight end's outside leg, and its biggest
  gains come from the edge being reached (the bounce) or the defense over-running the play (the cutback).

Now ask what kind of alignment makes each one hard.

::: {#cell-fig-front-vs-zone .cell execution_count=7}

The rule of thumb that falls out of @fig-front-vs-zone is simple to state:

- **To beat the double team, line up on top of or just inside the blockers.** A nose on the center and
  4is inside the tackles leave the offense's two uncovered linemen stuck on doubles; the pairs can't
  move their men and can't leave them. That is the tite's answer to inside zone and duo, the
  double-team runs. (Gap runs like power, as the last section showed, are a fight it wins with
  technique, not with alignment.)
- **To beat the reach, line up outside the blockers, and leave no gap empty on the edge.** A reach block
  is hardest when the defender is already a step to the play side of the blocker: a 3-technique outside
  the guard, a 5 outside the tackle, a 9 or a wide edge outside the tight end. Against outside zone the
  tite's problem isn't that its linemen are easy to reach; the 4i is actually a hard reach for the guard.
  It is that the C gap is empty, so the play-side tackle is free to help on the edge or climb to the lone
  linebacker, and that its biggest men have to run sideways. That is why the classic answer to an outside-zone
  team is a *wider* front, with shades outside the blockers, often a four-man even front with a 3-technique
  who can penetrate before the guard's reach lands, as in
  [Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)'s one-gap animation.

The two answers pull in opposite directions, which is why no front stops everything. A tite that pulls
its ends inside to choke inside zone has emptied the gaps outside the tackles that outside zone attacks; a
wide four-man front that beats the reach leaves the interior gaps to linebackers who can be climbed to.
Defenses solve the dilemma in three ways, and you can watch for all of them:

1. **Change the front by opponent.** A defense facing an inside-zone and duo team plays a lot of tite;
   the same defense facing a wide-zone team widens its edges and plays more four-man fronts. Fangio's own
   defenses varied in exactly this way: Alexander notes that in Denver Fangio favoured a four-down front
   more often than his former assistant Staley, who preferred the five-man front.[^denver]
2. **Change the front by down, distance and formation.** Tite on first-and-10 against two tight ends,
   four-man front on second-and-long against three receivers.
3. **Change the front after the offense lines up.** Shift from one to the other at the last moment, so the
   offense's blocking calls are made against the wrong picture. That is the last section of this chapter.

Who, in either front, makes the tackle on the run that gets through? That is the job of the run fits,
the full eleven-man accounting of who owns which gap and who forces the ball back inside, in
[Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

## Nickel fronts: 4-2-5, 3-3-5, 2-4-5

Everything so far has been about base defenses. But the modern NFL plays nickel, five defensive backs,
on most snaps: about 60 percent of all runs and passes in 2025, with base (four defensive backs) on
about 30 percent and dime on most of the rest.[^part] So the front you will see most often on Sunday
is a nickel front, and nickel fronts have their own three-number names. All three end in 5: five
defensive backs. The first two numbers split the other six players between the line and the
linebackers.

Why can't a 3-4 team just stay in its Okie against three receivers? Because the third receiver has to be
covered by somebody. In the Okie that somebody is an outside linebacker, who walks out from the end of
the line to stand over the slot. That leaves a four-man front in the box with one soft, empty edge where
he used to be, and a 250-pound rusher in coverage on a receiver. Taking a big man off for a nickel back,
and rebuilding the front from what is left, is the better trade. The three nickel fronts are the three
ways to rebuild it.

The [**4-2-5**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-4-2-5) is the even front with a linebacker swapped for a
nickel back: four down linemen, two linebackers, five defensive backs. It is the most natural answer to
three receivers, because it changes as little as possible. The four-man line is the same one the
defense plays in base, so the linemen's rules don't change; the two linebackers who stay on are the
Mike and the Will, the better athletes; and the nickel back takes the slot receiver the Sam would have
been chasing.

Count the box in @fig-425-2x2 and you will see why it holds up against the run as well as it does.
With the tight end split out, the offense has five blockers; the 4-2-5 has six in the box. One more
defender than blockers is the [plus-one](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-plus-one) idea of
[Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd), and the nickel at the apex makes a seventh
who can fill late. The offense's usual answers are to bring the tight end back in tight (six blockers),
or to read an unblocked defender with the quarterback, the
[option](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) principle, which turns the quarterback into the
extra man.

The [**2-4-5**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2-4-5) is what a 3-4 team usually plays when the
offense brings out a third receiver: the nose tackle comes off for a nickel back, the two ends slide
inside to play the tackle spots, and the two outside linebackers stay on the edges, standing. You met
it as a footnote in [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd);
look at it now in @fig-245, next to a 4-2-5, and the two are the same front. Four players on the line,
two linebackers behind them, five defensive backs. If the 2-4-5's outside linebackers put their hands
down, you couldn't tell them apart at all.

So why the different name? Because the name is built from the *roster*, not the picture. The 2-4-5's
edges are listed as linebackers because, in the team's base defense, they are the 3-4's outside
linebackers. Bring the same two players onto a 4-3 team and they would be listed as defensive ends, and
the identical alignment would be called a 4-2-5.

### 3-3-5: three meanings

The [**3-3-5**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-3-5) is three down linemen, three linebackers and
five defensive backs, and it is the one name in this section that means different things depending on
who says it.

- **When an NFL coach calls a 3-3-5 front,** he means a five-man line in nickel: three linemen inside, a
  stand-up edge on each end, and one linebacker behind them. The tite of @fig-tite-inside-zone is exactly
  this, the 3-4 team's nickel with its nose back on the field. It is the light-box run front of the Fangio
  tree, and the Staley branch of that tree calls it **Penny**, a nickel with a nose.[^penny]
- **When the roster count says 3-3-5,** it usually means something else: a four-man line with one edge
  listed as a defensive end and the other as a linebacker. That is what most of the 3-3-5 snaps in the
  data below are.
- **In college, "3-3-5" usually means the *3-3-5 stack*,** a different defense with three linemen and
  three linebackers stacked directly behind them, usually credited to Joe Lee Dunn at Memphis in 1991
  and spread in the 1990s as a way to put more speed on the field against spread offenses.[^stack] It
  belongs to [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).

Which one you are looking at, the hands will tell you: three down inside the tackles with an edge on
each side is the coach's 3-3-5; four men on the line is the roster's.

### The labels, measured

You can see how loosely these names attach to the football in the play-by-play data. Since 2023, the
nflverse participation file (charted by FTN) lists the roster position of every defender on every snap,
so each snap's personnel can be counted as linemen–linebackers–defensive backs. Here is every 2025
nickel snap, split by what the roster labels call it.

``` {.python .cell-code}
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

style.apply()


def split_personnel(s):
    """(DL, LB, DB) counts from an FTN-era string such as '3 CB, 2 DE, 2 DT, 1 FS, 1 MLB, 1 OLB, 1 SS'."""
    c = {}
    for v, k in re.findall(r"(\d+)\s+([A-Z]+)", str(s)):
        c[k] = c.get(k, 0) + int(v)
    dl = sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in ("DE", "DT", "NT", "DL"))
    lb = sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in ("OLB", "ILB", "MLB", "LB"))
    db = sum(c.get(k, 0) for k in ("CB", "FS", "SS", "S", "DB"))
    return dl, lb, db

    ["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "defense_personnel", "defenders_in_box", "number_of_pass_rushers"]]

cnt = snaps.defense_personnel.map(split_personnel)
snaps["dl"], snaps["lb"], snaps["db"] = [c[0] for c in cnt], [c[1] for c in cnt], [c[2] for c in cnt]
snaps = snaps[snaps.dl + snaps.lb + snaps.db == 11]
snaps["label"] = snaps.dl.astype(str) + "-" + snaps.lb.astype(str) + "-" + snaps.db.astype(str)

BASE_SHARE = (snaps.db == 4).mean()

ax.legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.13), ncol=4, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
```

Two things jump out of @fig-nickel-labels and the table under it. First, the league splits cleanly into
two camps, and the split has nothing to do with what the defenses do: it is about how teams list their
edge rushers. Teams whose edges are "defensive ends" play the 4-2-5; teams whose edges are "outside
linebackers" play the 2-4-5. Second, the three labels describe nearly identical football. All three put
about six defenders in the box, all three rush about four on passes, roughly three times in four exactly four.

That is why this book, and every coach you will read, asks you to **count hands, not names.** Before
the snap, count the players with a hand on the ground and the players standing at the ends of the line,
and note where the man nearest the center is. Four down is a four-man line, whatever the graphic says.
Two down with two standing edges is a four-man line too, built from 3-4 personnel. Three down inside
the tackles with an edge on each side is a tite, five on the line. The personnel label tells you which
players are on the field, which matters for what they *can* do (a 3-4 outside linebacker can drop into
coverage more comfortably than a 4-3 end); the alignment tells you what they are *about* to do.

## Multiple defenses: one personnel group, many fronts

If the label is personnel and the front is alignment, nothing stops a defense from playing several
fronts with the same eleven players. Almost every NFL defense now does. A
[**multiple defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-multiple-defense) (also called a
[**hybrid defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hybrid-defense)) lines up in more than one front
family, odd and even, four-man and five-man, often from the same personnel and sometimes switching
between them before the snap. "Now every team is 'multiple,'" one analyst wrote more than a decade
ago, and it has only become more true.[^multiple]

Belichick's Patriots were the model of the idea: a defense that might be a two-gap 3-4 one week and a
four-man front the next, built to take away whatever the opponent did best. The modern versions go
further, changing fronts *within* a series, and the most effective way to do it is a shift: show the
offense one front, then move into another as the quarterback is calling the protection.

::: {#cell-fig-same-personnel-two-fronts .cell execution_count=12}

Same eleven players, two fronts (simulated; dark dots are hands on the ground; each lineman's label is his technique, and it changes when he moves). The defense is in 4-2-5 nickel personnel (four defensive linemen) against a shotgun one-back set with the tight end (Y) attached on the right. 1: it shows a four-man even front: four hands down, a wide 5 on the left, a 3, a 1, and a 5 on the right tackle, with the Mike and Will behind them. 2: as the quarterback calls his protection, the front shifts. The 1 slides onto the center; the 3 and the right end both slide to 4is, the end keeping his hand down; the left end (ringed) stands up and widens: the edge who changes stance. The Mike (ringed) walks up outside the tight end. 3: at the snap, five on the line, three hands down, all three inside the tackles: a tite, and every interior spot is still held by a defensive lineman. 4: the offense passes. Four rush (the three linemen and the standing left edge), and the walked-up Mike drops into the flat: a front that showed five on the line rushed four, and the player who looked like a rusher is in coverage.
:::
:::


Why go to that trouble? Because, as [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) explained,
an offensive line decides its blocking before the snap: who is covered, who doubles, who climbs, and,
on a pass, which way the center slides and who picks up which rusher. A front that shifts at the last
moment makes those decisions against the wrong picture. In @fig-same-personnel-two-fronts the line set
its rules against a four-man even front with two linebackers; at the snap it faced a five-man line
with one, and on the pass, the player it had counted as a rusher (the walked-up Mike) was in coverage.
Notice what the shift does *not* do: it never puts a 250-pound edge rusher on a tackle's inside shoulder.
Every interior spot of the tite is still held by a defensive lineman; the only man who changes stance is
the end who stands up on the outside. Georgia's defense under Kirby Smart is known for exactly this
move, from a 4-2-5 into its mint front without a substitution: one tackle to the nose, the other tackle
and an end to 4is, the other end standing up and walking out.[^georgia]

The cost of being multiple is complexity. Every front has its own gap assignments and its own fits, and
every player has to know all of them; a shift that is a beat late leaves a gap empty at the snap. That
is why multiple defenses are built around smart, versatile players (edges who can rush and drop,
linemen who can play a 3 and a 4i) and why they live and die on the communication of the
[green-dot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-green-dot) linebacker who relays the call.

## Dialect: Okie, Eagle, G, and the problem with names

You now know what the fronts *are*. A word about what they are *called*, because front names are the
least standardized vocabulary in football. Every staff has a language, inherited from the coaches who
trained its coaches, and the same word can mean different things in neighbouring buildings. Two names
you will hear are good examples.

::: {#cell-fig-dialect .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
DIALECT = [("Okie", [("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)], ()),
           ("Eagle (one dialect)", [("LE", "4i", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4i", 1)], ("LE", "RE")),
           ("G: nose on a guard", [("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "2i", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)], ("NT",))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.1))
for ax, (ttl, spec, moved) in zip(axes, DIALECT):
    dfn = front(spec, lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.1, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 2.1, "M")],
                others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -6.2, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.2, "E")])
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in moved:
        p.highlight(k, color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.1, 8.3), window=(-4.6, 7.0), title=False)
    hands(f, p, ("LE", "NT", "RE"))
    if "G" in ttl:      # the uncovered center has to step sideways to reach the 2i
        point_to(f, p, (-3.2, -3.6), (-0.8, -0.2), "C now steps\nsideways", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
                 fontsize=6.5, shrink=5)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```
